name: andreykaravaev.ru
object_type: Portfolio, but functionally a one-person freelance shop-front. It carries all the usual portfolio furniture (hero, project list, about, contact) and then bolts on something a portfolio normally lacks: a 35-question client-intake instrument at `/tor_builder.html` that generates a formatted technical specification (ТЗ / terms of reference), collects budget and deadline, and hands the result to Telegram. That single feature shifts the object from 'here is my work' toward 'here is how you start a project with me'. It is not a consulting-company site (no company entity, no services page, no rates card, no testimonials), not a template or OSS repo (though its own source happens to be public), and not an aggregator.
format_genre: Scroll-page as the primary genre, with a genuine terminal-CLI set piece embedded in it, plus a separate multi-step form application on a second route. The home page is a four-section vertical scroll (hero → portfolio → about → CTA) driven by Lenis smooth scrolling, with a WebGL canvas in the CTA block and a canvas starfield behind the page. The About section is not prose at all — it is a macOS-styled terminal window (`~/profile — zsh`, traffic-light dots, prompt `andrey@portfolio:~$`) that types out four commands and their output when scrolled into view. The `/tor_builder.html` route is a different genre entirely: a blueprint-grid-styled wizard with a progress bar and ten tick marks, closer to a SaaS onboarding flow than to a portfolio page. So the terminal aesthetic is a section-level device and a styling vocabulary (monospace, `//` comments, `НА_ГЛАВНУЮ` in caps-with-underscore, `[ ... ]` bracketed taglines) rather than a whole-site OS simulation — the site does not ask you to type anything to navigate.
intent_audience: Freelance client acquisition, stated unambiguously and structurally, not just in copy. The main nav's fourth item is literally 'Нанять' (Hire). The hero tagline is a service promise rather than a self-description: 'Берусь за задание целиком — от старта до проекта под ключ. После релиза помогаю поддерживать продукт' (I take the whole job — from start to a turnkey project. After release I help maintain the product). The primary CTA, repeated in the hero, the mobile nav and a dedicated full-width CTA section, is 'Составить ТЗ за 10 минут →' (Build a spec in 10 minutes), and the CTA section's kicker is '// Готов к работе' (ready to work). The intake flow asks for budget with a stated floor ('Минимальная стоимость — 1 000 рублей') and for a preferred contact channel — the two questions a job-seeker never asks and a freelancer always does. Audience is Russian-language small-business and individual buyers who have an idea but no specification: the CTA copy addresses exactly that pain ('Составление технического задания может занять время, но без него проект теряет форму еще до старта… с нуля, без опыта, прямо в браузере'). Secondary signals of a job-seeking or personal-brand motive are weak-to-absent: no CV, no availability-for-hire-as-employee statement, no blog, no talks, no newsletter. Not gated — the intake tool is fully open and requires no email to use.
seniority_stage: Student / junior in years, but the site is positioned as a working freelancer — and the age is disclosed rather than hidden. The terminal's `whoami` output states it plainly: 'Андрей Караваев — fullstack-разработчик, 16 лет' (fullstack developer, 16 years old), with 'Специализация: frontend, backend, системное программирование, кибербезопасность'. The evidence base matches a strong, fast-moving hobbyist-to-early-professional: two hackathon results with downloadable certificates (2nd place at 'Кибер Рывок', participation in Nuclear IT Hack, both 2026), one paid commercial delivery, a GitHub account created 2024-05-24 with 12 public repositories and 4 followers, and a real technical range across Python/FastAPI/Flask, Rust/Axum/Tokio, TypeScript and PostgreSQL. What 'good' means for this item is unusual and worth stating precisely: because the intent is client acquisition rather than employment, the site is judged on whether it can make a paying stranger comfortable — and the age disclosure cuts against that, while the certificates, the public source code, the privacy policy and the spec-builder all cut in favour. The site's structural choice is telling: the age appears in a typed terminal animation two-thirds down the page, after the work has already been shown. There is no attempt to imply seniority anywhere — no 'X years of experience', no invented job titles, no client logo wall.
language_i18n: Russian only, with an English typographic veneer and no i18n mechanism. `<html lang="ru">` on the home page, `/tor_builder.html` and `/privacy.html`; all navigation, project copy, terminal output, the entire 35-question intake flow, the generated specification, and the privacy policy are in Russian. There is no EN/RU toggle, no `/en` route, no `hreflang`, and no locale meta (`og:locale` is absent entirely). English is used decoratively and inconsistently: the role label 'Fullstack Developer' under the Russian `<h1>`, the footer wordmark 'Andrey Karavaev' in Latin script, all five project names (VORTEX, Artifex, Orbityx, HotFix — only 'Приёмка квартир' is Russian), and every technology tag. Two small correctness bugs in the same area: `/qr_code.html` declares `lang="en"` while containing only Russian text, and the home page ships no `og:title`, `og:description`, `og:url` or `og:type` at all — only `og:image` pointing at an SVG (with `og:image:type` declared as `image/svg+xml` at 1200×630, which most social platforms will not render), so link previews will fall back to the raw `<title>` 'Обо мне' ('About me'). For a site whose whole purpose is inbound client acquisition, shareable-link metadata being broken is a more consequential gap than the missing English.
url: https://andreykaravaev.ru — canonical and fully working over HTTPS (HTTP/2, valid certificate, GitHub Pages + Fastly edge). Three additional first-party routes matter for research: https://andreykaravaev.ru/tor_builder.html (the spec builder, the site's primary CTA), https://andreykaravaev.ru/privacy.html (nine-part privacy policy, last updated April 2026), and https://andreykaravaev.ru/qr_code.html (share page with a QR code for the domain). No robots.txt and no sitemap.xml (both 404 into a custom 404 page). Note the site never declares a `<link rel="canonical">` and ships no `og:url`, so the canonical origin is asserted only by DNS and the Pages custom-domain configuration.
owner_role: Andrey Karavaev (Андрей Караваев; full legal name Караваев Андрей Александрович, disclosed via the linked award certificates) — self-labelled 'Fullstack Developer' in the hero and in his GitHub bio. The terminal's `whoami` output expands this to 'fullstack-разработчик, 16 лет' with 'Специализация: frontend, backend, системное программирование, кибербезопасность' (frontend, backend, systems programming, cybersecurity). Stated interests reinforce a systems/security bent rather than a web-agency one: 'Blockchain-разработка · Rust-экосистема', 'Кибербезопасность · P2P-сети · Fullstack-разработка', plus hackathons and open source. Working stack, per the terminal's `stack` command: Python · FastAPI · Flask · SQLAlchemy / Rust · Axum · PostgreSQL · Tokio / JavaScript · WebSocket · WebRTC. Positioning is that of an independent contractor rather than a candidate — 'Берусь за задание целиком — от старта до проекта под ключ' (I take the whole job, from start to turnkey) — with no employer, education institution, agency or client company named anywhere on the site. GitHub: `Andre-wb`, name field 'Andrey', bio 'Fullstack Developer', blog field pointing back at andreykaravaev.ru, account created 2024-05-24, 12 public repositories, 4 followers.
sections_present: Home page: four sections plus a footer. About — YES, but rendered as terminal output rather than prose (see nav_pattern/format_genre): `whoami` gives name, age and specialisation; `stack` prints three grouped technology lines; `achievements` prints the two hackathon results and the commercial order; `interests` prints Blockchain/Rust ecosystem, cybersecurity, P2P networks, fullstack, hackathons and open source. Projects — YES ('Портфолио', 5 numbered entries, the largest section). Skills — YES, in two places: per-project technology tags, and the terminal's `stack` output (Python · FastAPI · Flask · SQLAlchemy / Rust · Axum · PostgreSQL · Tokio / JavaScript · WebSocket · WebRTC). Contact — YES, distributed rather than sectioned: a social row in the hero, a Telegram button in the CTA block, and a Contacts column in the footer. Experience — NO: no employment history, no client list, no timeline, no durations; the closest substitute is the `achievements` terminal output and the per-project status badges. Resume/CV — NO (no PDF, no inline CV, no external CV link; the only PDFs on the site are the two hackathon certificates). Blog — NO. Beyond the checklist there are three additional routes and one overlay that carry real weight: `/tor_builder.html` (the 35-question spec builder — effectively a second product), `/privacy.html` (a nine-part privacy policy with its own table of contents, last updated April 2026), `/qr_code.html` (a 'Поделиться'/share page showing a QR code for the domain — a nod to handing the site out in person), and a full-screen gallery modal with pinch-zoom that serves screenshots for all five projects.
nav_pattern: Single-page anchor scroll for content, with three genuine sub-pages hanging off it. A fixed header holds four anchor links (Главная / Проекты / Обо мне / Нанять) on desktop; below the breakpoint they collapse into a burger menu (`aria-label="Меню"`, `aria-expanded` maintained) which opens an overlay containing the same four links plus a highlighted 'Составить ТЗ' entry and three social links — so the mobile menu is a superset of the desktop nav and is the only place the primary CTA appears in the navigation. Scrolling is intercepted by Lenis (`lenis@1.1.9` from unpkg) for inertial smooth scroll, with `js/smooth_scroll.js` wiring anchors into it. The footer repeats the section nav, adds a five-item deep-link list to individual project anchors (`#vortex`, `#artifex`, `#orbityx`, `#realestate`, `#hotfix`), links the share/QR page, and links the privacy policy. Sub-pages are conventional multi-page navigation: `/tor_builder.html` replaces the site chrome with its own top bar (a 'НА_ГЛАВНУЮ' link, a progress track with ten tick marks, a step counter '01 / 01' and a back button), and `/privacy.html` has a 'Вернуться на главную' link and an internal table of contents. Project galleries are modal overlays with prev/next buttons, dot indicators and a counter — they do not change the URL, so an individual screenshot is not linkable.
visual_style: Dark 'developer terminal / blueprint' aesthetic, executed consistently and with more restraint than the feature list suggests. The base is near-black (#03050b) with layered surfaces (#0b0e17, #141a29) and blue hairline borders (`rgba(88,166,255,0.12)`) — the GitHub-dark colour family. Design-trend alignment: terminal-inspired above all (the macOS window chrome with traffic-light dots, monospace throughout the UI, `//` comment prefixes on headings such as '// Готов к работе' and '// Техническое задание готово', caps-with-underscore link labels), layered over a restrained dark-glass/depth treatment (translucent surfaces, blue glow shadows `0 24px 80px -8px`, a `.bp-grid` blueprint grid backdrop on the spec builder marked `aria-hidden`). It is not a bento grid, not neo-brutalist, not glassmorphism in the frosted sense, and not kinetic typography. Three bespoke visual systems do the differentiating work: (1) per-project CSS/DOM 'visuals' that illustrate each project abstractly instead of using a screenshot as the card image — an animated node mesh for the P2P messenger, an orbital system for the school diary, a 3D-CSS extruded building for the property-inspection site, a green/red candlestick chart for the crypto tracker, and a sweeping radar screen for the Rust debugging platform; (2) a canvas starfield behind the page (`js/stars.js`); and (3) a Three.js WebGL canvas in the CTA section (`js/cta_shapes.js`). The per-project abstract visuals are the smartest choice here: they give the card grid a distinct identity per project at near-zero asset weight, while the real screenshots live one click deeper in the gallery modal.
color_typography: Dark-only; there is no light theme and no toggle. The site does declare both `theme-color` values for browser chrome (`#1a1a2e` for dark, `#f5f5f7` for light) via `prefers-color-scheme` media attributes, but no `prefers-color-scheme` rule exists in any stylesheet — so the light value affects only the browser UI, never the page. Palette is defined as CSS custom properties in `css/base.css`: `--bg #03050b`, `--surface #0b0e17`, `--surface2 #141a29`, `--border rgba(88,166,255,.12)` / `--border-hi rgba(88,166,255,.3)`, `--accent #3b82f6` (blue) with `--accent2 #00e1ff` (cyan) and `--accent-glow rgba(59,130,246,.4)`, semantic `--green #10b981` / `--red #ef4444` (used for the candlestick visual and form states), `--text #fff`, `--muted #94a3b8`, `--muted2 #5f6c84`, radii 14/20px. Typography is a two-face system, self-hosted as VARIABLE TTF files rather than woff2 — 'Unbounded' (a geometric display face, weights 200–900) for headings and UI, and 'JetBrains Mono' for terminal, code and label text, both with `font-display: swap`. Shipping variable TTF instead of woff2 is the single biggest avoidable weight problem on the site: Unbounded-VariableFont_wght.ttf is 777 KB and JetBrainsMono-VariableFont_wght.ttf is 189 KB, a combined 966 KB that woff2 subsetting would cut by roughly 80–90%. Inconsistently, `/tor_builder.html` abandons both faces and loads a different pair from Google Fonts (Space Mono + IBM Plex Sans), so the primary conversion page does not match the brand typography of the site that feeds it. Contrast: white-on-#03050b body text is strong; `--muted2 #5f6c84` on the dark surface is the weakest pairing and is used for secondary metadata.
motion: Motion-heavy by portfolio standards, and — to the author's credit — explicitly gated for reduced-motion users at the CSS layer, with a genuinely sophisticated adaptive-quality system on top. What moves: Lenis inertial smooth scrolling site-wide; a canvas starfield; scroll-triggered reveals and project slide-in animations (`js/animations.js`, `js/projects_slide_animation.js`) driven by IntersectionObserver; the About terminal, which types character-by-character with randomised per-character delay (68ms + up to 40ms jitter), simulates a `pip install` progress sequence and a braille spinner (`⠋⠙⠹⠸⠼⠴⠦⠧⠇⠏`) for a fake 'Загрузка достижений...' load, and is triggered once at 25% visibility; a blinking block cursor; and a Three.js r128 WebGL scene in the CTA section. `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` IS respected, with an intentional comment in `css/base.css` explaining why ('Пользователи Firefox на Windows часто включают «уменьшить движение» в настройках ОС. Уважаем это') and a global override setting `animation-duration: 0.01ms !important`, `animation-iteration-count: 1 !important`, `transition-duration: 0.01ms !important` and `scroll-behavior: auto !important` on `*, ::before, ::after`. The important limitation: that block only reaches CSS animation. The JS-driven motion is NOT gated — no script queries `prefers-reduced-motion` anywhere, so with reduce enabled the Lenis smooth scroll still hijacks scrolling, the starfield still animates, the WebGL shapes still spin, and the terminal still types out character by character. Since the terminal is the only place the About content exists, it cannot simply be disabled — but it should render instantly rather than type. Offsetting this, `js/cta_shapes.js` implements a real adaptive-performance tier system that most portfolios do not attempt: it classifies the device as low/medium/high from `navigator.hardwareConcurrency`, `navigator.deviceMemory`, `navigator.getBattery()` (dropping to power-save mode below 20% charge or when `saveData` is set), a low-end-device user-agent regex (Samsung SM-A1/SM-J, Redmi 0–6, Moto E/G, Realme, Android 4–8), iOS versions below 15, and small-viewport detection; then measures live FPS with `requestAnimationFrame`, computes frame-time variance to detect thermal throttling, and dynamically lowers render scale (`adaptiveScale` 0.5–1.0) when frames drop.
responsiveness_mobile: Responsive and mobile-considered in the details, with one clear accessibility violation. The layout reflows properly (CSS breakpoint at 768px, `matchMedia('(max-width: 768px)')` in the gallery script), desktop nav collapses to a burger with an overlay, and the format_genre degrades cleanly: the terminal window is a fluid-width box that scrolls internally (`terminal.scrollTop = terminal.scrollHeight` after each line) rather than forcing horizontal page scroll, and the terminal output lines are short enough to wrap. Three mobile-specific engineering decisions stand out. First, the gallery serves separate mobile image variants — `getImageUrl()` appends `_m.png` instead of `.png` below 768px, and the difference is large (vortex1.png is 1.81 MB while vortex1_m.png is 397 KB), so the heaviest content on the site is genuinely halved-and-then-some for phones. Second, the gallery implements a full touch interaction model: pinch-to-zoom with `initialPinchDistance`/`initialScale` tracking, double-tap-to-zoom with tap-position memory, drag-to-pan with rAF-throttled updates, and passive event listeners. Third, the WebGL CTA scene degrades via the device-tier system described under motion (low-end UA patterns, small-screen detection, battery-aware power-save, adaptive render scale). THE VIOLATION: the home page's viewport meta is `width=device-width, user-scalable=no, initial-scale=1.0, maximum-scale=1.0, minimum-scale=1.0` — it disables pinch-zoom on the entire page, which fails WCAG 1.4.4 (Resize Text) and is exactly the wrong choice for users who need magnification. It is also internally inconsistent, since `/tor_builder.html` correctly allows `maximum-scale=5.0`, and since the gallery modal goes to considerable trouble to implement its own pinch-zoom — i.e. zoom was disabled globally and then hand-reimplemented for images only. Removing `user-scalable=no` and the scale clamps from the home page is a one-line fix. [uncertain — layout behaviour is inferred from the served CSS/JS and breakpoints rather than verified on a physical device or emulator.]
framework_hosting: No framework and no generator — hand-written static HTML, vanilla ES5/ES6 JavaScript in IIFEs and classes, and plain CSS with custom properties. Structure is deliberate rather than accidental: `css/main.css` is a 537-byte aggregator that `@import`s eight partials (base, header, intro, projects, about, cookie, footer) with a comment explaining that existing `<link href="css/main.css">` references keep working, and the JavaScript is split into ten single-purpose files (animations, slider, smooth_scroll, projects_slide_animation, stars, terminal, burger, cookies, cta_shapes, prefix) plus `tor.js` for the spec builder. Two third-party libraries are loaded from CDNs rather than bundled: `lenis@1.1.9` from unpkg (13.6 KB) and Three.js **r128** from cdnjs (603 KB) — r128 dates from 2021, is roughly five years and ~50 releases behind, and is the full non-tree-shaken build pulled in for a single decorative CTA canvas. Both are `<script>` tags without `defer` or `async`, so they are render-blocking (only the six first-party scripts that can be deferred are). Hosting is GitHub Pages, confirmed by response headers: `server: GitHub.com`, Fastly edge (`via: 1.1 varnish`, `x-served-by: cache-ams-eham8680062-AMS`, `x-cache: HIT`, `x-fastly-request-id`), `cache-control: max-age=600`, HTTP/2, valid TLS. The publishing repository is `github.com/Andre-wb/portfolio` (`has_pages: true`, JavaScript, last pushed 2026-06-22 — matching the `last-modified: Mon, 22 Jun 2026 14:38:54 GMT` on the served document). Custom domain `andreykaravaev.ru`: full personal name on the Russian ccTLD, correctly attached to Pages with working HTTPS — a clean, credible setup for a client-facing site. One architectural consequence of the static host is load-bearing: `js/tor.js` declares `const BOT_API_URL = '/send-tor'`, an origin-relative POST endpoint that GitHub Pages cannot serve (verified: `GET /send-tor` → 404, `POST /send-tor` → 405). That path is a vestige of a dynamic backend that does not exist here; see project_presentation/standout_features for how the flow survives it. Also absent: no robots.txt and no sitemap.xml (both 404 into the custom 404 page).
performance_a11y:
PERFORMANCE: functionally slow on first load for reasons that are all fixable, and none of which are the site's actual features. Measured critical path for the home page is roughly 2.4 MB uncompressed: 876 KB of first-party assets (a 22.7 KB HTML document, ~53 KB across nine CSS partials, ~72 KB across ten JS files, and a **726 KB unoptimised PNG portrait**), plus **966 KB of variable TTF fonts** (Unbounded 777 KB + JetBrains Mono 189 KB), plus **617 KB of CDN JavaScript** (Three.js r128 603 KB + Lenis 13.6 KB). Three items — the portrait PNG, the TTF fonts and Three.js r128 — account for about 95% of the weight, and every one has a cheap remedy: convert the portrait to WebP/AVIF at display size (a plausible 20–40× reduction), subset the fonts to woff2, and either import only the needed Three.js modules from a current version or replace the decorative canvas with CSS. Compounding this, the two CDN scripts are render-blocking (no `defer`/`async`) and come from two additional origins (unpkg, cdnjs) requiring separate DNS/TLS handshakes with no `preconnect`. The CSS `@import` chain adds a second round-trip before any partial is even discovered. There is no `loading="lazy"` anywhere, and the gallery's desktop screenshots are 1.5–2.1 MB PNGs each (vortex1.png 1.81 MB, artifex1.png 1.56 MB, orbityx2.png 2.08 MB) — mitigated only by being fetched on modal open and by the `_m.png` mobile variants. On the credit side: GitHub Pages + Fastly gives fast global edge delivery with HTTP/2, the JS is small and dependency-free, `font-display: swap` avoids invisible text, and the adaptive-quality tier system genuinely protects low-end devices at runtime. ACCESSIBILITY: thin, with one real violation and one real strength. Violation — `user-scalable=no, maximum-scale=1.0` on the home page blocks pinch-zoom (WCAG 1.4.4). Strength — a deliberate, commented `prefers-reduced-motion` implementation (CSS-layer only; JS motion is ungated). Otherwise sparse: a correct single `

` with sensible `h2`/`h3` descent (1/3/6), `lang="ru"` set, `aria-label` on the burger with `aria-expanded` maintained and `aria-label` on the gallery close button (3 `aria-*` attributes total), a meaningful `alt` on the one ``, and `aria-hidden` on the decorative blueprint grid. analytics_instrumentation: None, and — unusually — the site says so and means it. No Google Analytics or gtag, no Google Tag Manager, no Yandex.Metrica (notable for a Russian-market commercial site, where Metrica is close to default), no VK retargeting pixel, no Plausible, Umami, Fathom, Vercel Analytics, Microsoft Clarity, or session-replay tooling — verified by scanning the home page, the spec builder and the privacy policy for all of the above. The privacy policy states it directly: 'Сайт не использует счётчики аналитики и не передаёт данные рекламным системам' and 'Сайт не использует рекламные, аналитические или отслеживающие технологии от третьих сторон'. There IS a cookie/consent banner, which at first looks contradictory, but the policy explains it honestly: the only client-side storage is `localStorage` — `tor_quiz_v5` holding spec-builder progress so answers survive an accidental tab close, and `cookie_consent_v1` recording the consent choice so the banner does not reappear. The banner text says exactly that ('Я использую cookie для сохранения прогресса при составлении ТЗ и фиксации вашего согласия. Данные не передаются рекламным системам'). The policy additionally discloses the client-side device profiling used for graphics quality (CPU core count, a timing-based performance probe, WebGL capability) and states that it is used only for effect tuning. Trade-off: with no analytics the owner cannot see how many visitors start the spec builder versus finish it — the one funnel metric that would matter most for a lead-generation site — but the absence is a coherent, documented privacy stance rather than an oversight.
project_presentation:
Five projects in a numbered vertical card list under the heading 'Портфолио', each card structured identically: a two-part meta row (a zero-padded number 01–05 and a **status badge** naming the project's provenance), a name, a 1–2 sentence description that leads with technical substance, five technology tags, a links row, and a bespoke animated CSS/DOM visual in place of a thumbnail.

THE STATUS-BADGE TAXONOMY is the sharpest content idea on the site — five projects, five honestly differentiated provenances: '01 VORTEX — Хакатон · Участие' (hackathon, participation), '02 Artifex — Хакатон · 2 место' (hackathon, 2nd place), '03 Приёмка квартир — Коммерческий' (commercial), '04 Orbityx — Пет-проект' (pet project), '05 HotFix — Соло проект' (solo project). A reader instantly knows which work was paid, which was competitive, which was for fun, and which was solo versus team — information most portfolios flatten into a uniform grid.

THE ENTRIES: (1) VORTEX — decentralised P2P messenger with E2E encryption that works without internet on a local network; Rust crypto core, WebRTC video calls, multi-hop routing; tags Python, FastAPI, Rust, AES-GCM, X25519. (2) Artifex — school electronic diary with two-factor auth, a custom CSRF defence and a grades tracker; explicitly credited as 'Командный проект, руководил разработкой' (team project, led development); tags Python, FastAPI, JWT, WAF, SQLAlchemy. (3) Приёмка квартир — the paid job: a portfolio site for an apartment-handover inspector with 3D effects, a file-upload form, Telegram-bot and email notification integration; tags Python, Flask, TeleBot, SMTP, 3D CSS. (4) Orbityx — real-time cryptocurrency tracker with a custom TypeScript candlestick-charting library supporting drawing, AI forecasting and user-defined indicators; tags Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, WebSocket, ASGI. (5) HotFix — a learning platform for Rust developers with find-and-fix-the-bug exercises, progress statistics, 2FA and a sandboxed Docker container; tags Rust, Axum, PostgreSQL, Docker, JS.

EVIDENCE LAYER — SCREENSHOTS YES, LIVE DEMOS NO. Four of five link to a public GitHub repository (Vortex, Artifex, Orbityx, HotFix; the commercial project correctly has no repo, as client work usually cannot). All four repos exist and are active: `Andre-wb/Vortex` (JS, pushed 2026-07-25), `Andre-wb/Artifex` (Python, 4 stars, 2026-03-04), `Andre-wb/Orbityx` (Python, 2026-03-27), `Andre-wb/HotFix` (Rust, 2026-06-05). Every one of the five also opens a **gallery modal** with real interface screenshots — 10 for Vortex, 6 each for Artifex, HotFix, Приёмка квартир and Orbityx, 34 in total — with prev/next controls, dot indicators, an 'n / m' counter, pinch/double-tap zoom, drag-to-pan and dedicated `_m.png` mobile variants. LIVE-DEMO AVAILABILITY IS ZERO: not one project links to a running deployment — no Vercel, Netlify, Fly, Render, HF Space or self-hosted demo. For the P2P messenger and the Docker-sandboxed Rust platform that is defensible (neither is trivially demoable), and for the commercial site the client presumably owns the URL, but Orbityx (a crypto chart viewer) and Artifex (a web diary) are both natural demo candidates. The gallery is a strong substitute for a portfolio aimed at non-technical buyers — a prospective client cares far more about seeing the interface than about running it — but it means every functional claim ('AI forecasting', 'multi-hop routing', 'custom CSRF defence') rests on a screenshot plus a repo the buyer will not read. There are no per-project case-study pages, no problem/approach/outcome narrative, no dates, and no client testimonial for the one commercial delivery.
resume_integration_mode: None of the four modes — and for this site that is a deliberate genre choice rather than a gap. There is no PDF CV, no inline HTML resume, nothing ATS-parseable, and no link to hh.ru, LinkedIn or Habr Career. The two PDFs on the site are award certificates, not a resume (see proof_verifiability). The functional substitute is the terminal's `whoami` + `stack` + `achievements` + `interests` sequence, which delivers the CV payload — name, age, specialisation, three technology groups, two hackathon results, one commercial engagement, and interests — but delivers it as JavaScript-generated text typed in over roughly 15 seconds. Consequences: it is not copy-pasteable in practice, not extractable by any parser, and entirely invisible without JavaScript, since the served HTML contains only an empty terminal box with a blinking cursor. There is also no experience section, no dated timeline and no education entry anywhere on the site. Because the target is clients rather than recruiters, the absence of an ATS-friendly CV costs little — a buyer wants a spec and a price, not a resume — but the same content being trapped inside an animation also means search engines and link previews see none of it.
proof_verifiability: THE STRONGEST PROOF LAYER OF ANY SITE IN THIS COHORT, and the pattern most worth copying: the two award claims are not badges or assertions but LINKED, DOWNLOADABLE, VERIFIABLE PDF CERTIFICATES, embedded directly in the terminal's `achievements` output. Both were fetched and their text extracted, and both check out. (1) `assets/кибер_рывок.pdf` (59 KB) is a 'ГРАМОТА' (certificate of merit) issued by the Faculty of Digital Industrial Technologies of SPbGMTU (St Petersburg State Marine Technical University), signed by dean A. A. Zhilenkov, awarded 'ЗА 2 МЕСТО' (for 2nd place) in the online hackathon 'КИБЕР РЫВОК' within the 'Программирование' track, to team **ARTIFEX**, naming four members: Караваев Андрей Александрович, Мальцев Борис Иванович, Афанасьев Леонид Андреевич, Абдувалиев Дониёрбек. (2) `assets/nuclear_it_hack.pdf` (883 KB) names Караваев Андрей Александрович and the team Artifex, corroborating the Nuclear IT Hack participation claim. The site's project card for Artifex says 'Хакатон · 2 место' and 'Командный проект, руководил разработкой' — the certificate independently confirms both the placement and that it was a four-person team, so the leadership claim is the only unverified part and is framed as a role rather than as sole authorship. That is honest attribution done properly. Supporting verifiability elsewhere is good but thinner: four of five projects link to real, active public repositories, so the code claims are inspectable by anyone who wants to; the 34 interface screenshots are self-evidencing for the existence of working UIs. THE GAPS: the 'Коммерческий заказ' (commercial order) claim in the terminal and the 'Коммерческий' badge on project 03 have no verification at all — no client name, no live URL, no testimonial, no invoice-adjacent evidence — which is the one claim a prospective paying client would most want corroborated. No project links a live deployment, so functional claims ('AI forecasting', 'multi-hop routing', 'works without internet on a local network', 'custom CSRF defence', 'sandboxed Docker container') are not independently testable without reading source. And one small precision note: the certificate specifies an ONLINE hackathon, while the site says only 'хакатон' — not a misstatement, but the certificate is more specific than the claim. Net: the site sets a genuinely high bar on the awards and then does not apply it to the commercial work.
quantified_impact: Sparse — competitive placements and capability claims, essentially no outcome metrics. The real quantities: 2nd place at 'Кибер Рывок' (2026), participation at Nuclear IT Hack (2026), one commercial order, five portfolio projects, four members on the winning hackathon team (available only from the certificate, not stated on the site), 'fullstack-разработчик, 16 лет', a '10 minutes' promise on the spec builder (a time-to-complete claim about the tool, not a project metric), and a stated minimum project budget of 1,000 RUB in the intake flow. What is absent is everything a client actually buys on: no user or install counts for any project, no uptime or latency figures for the FastAPI/Axum services, no throughput for the WebSocket crypto tracker, no dataset sizes, no revenue or cost-saving figure for the commercial delivery, no delivery-time or on-time-completion record, no number of clients served, and no repeat-business or satisfaction signal. The commercial project — the single most persuasive item for a buyer — is described purely by feature list ('3D эффекты, форма с прикреплением файлов, интеграция Telegram-бота и email-уведомлений') with no result, no client, and no 'delivered in N weeks'. GitHub supplies a modest external quantification the site does not use: 12 public repositories and 4 followers, with per-repo stars in the 1–4 range. For a freelance shop-front, adding even one outcome sentence to the commercial project ('delivered in N weeks; the client now receives inquiries via Telegram instead of phone') would move more than any visual feature on the page.
content_freshness: Fresh, with a visible and quantifiable lag between the code and the site. On-site signals: '© 2026 Андрей Караваев' in the footer, both hackathon achievements explicitly dated '[2026]' in the terminal output, and the privacy policy stamped 'Последнее обновление: апрель 2026 года'. Server signals: the served document carries `last-modified: Mon, 22 Jun 2026 14:38:54 GMT`, matching the last push to the publishing repo `Andre-wb/portfolio` (2026-06-22) — so the site was last edited about five and a half weeks before research. The lag: the owner's GitHub has moved on visibly in that window. `Andre-wb/Stellarix` (Rust, 4 stars — his most-starred repo, described as a decentralised offline messenger with voice communication) was pushed **2026-07-30, the day of research**, and `Dataset-for-StellarixAI` on 2026-07-25; neither appears anywhere on the site, and Stellarix looks like the successor to the VORTEX entry that occupies slot 01. Two further repos absent from the site (`near-tools`, a Near SDK in Rust, and `lethalhome`) suggest the portfolio selection is curated rather than exhaustive, which is fine — but the flagship omission is not curation, it is staleness. There is no 'currently working on' indicator, no changelog, no 'last updated' line, and no dates on any project card, so a visitor cannot tell how current the work is; the only reason the site reads as recent is the 2026 copyright and the dated achievements. Because the site is on GitHub Pages from a repo the owner pushes to regularly, closing this gap is a content task, not an engineering one.
writing_tone: Confident, service-oriented and technically plain — the voice of someone selling delivery rather than describing themselves, with a dry terminal-native register in the About section. Three notes. (1) COMMITMENT-FIRST in the client-facing copy: the hero tagline is a promise about scope and aftercare rather than a self-label — 'Берусь за задание целиком — от старта до проекта под ключ. После релиза помогаю поддерживать продукт' — and the CTA section names the client's problem before naming the solution: 'Составление технического задания может занять время, но без него проект теряет форму еще до старта… с нуля, без опыта, прямо в браузере' (building a spec takes time, but without one a project loses shape before it starts… from scratch, with no experience, right in the browser). That is unusually well-targeted copy: it addresses the buyer's anxiety, not the developer's credentials. (2) TERSE AND SPECIFIC in the project descriptions, which lead with mechanism rather than adjectives — 'Криптоядро на Rust, WebRTC видеозвонки, мультихоп-маршрутизация', 'двухфакторная аутентификация, собственная CRSF-защита', 'безопасный docker-контейнер'. There is no marketing inflation, no 'passionate about', no 'innovative solutions'. A single typo betrays the speed: 'CRSF-защита' for CSRF (and a Russian comment elsewhere reads 'автоматичекси'). (3) MATTER-OF-FACT rather than humorous in the terminal — the `whoami` output states the age flatly and moves on, and the `achievements` list uses emoji markers (🥈 🏆 💼) as structure rather than as jokes. The register is machine-voiced by design: `//` comment prefixes on headings ('// Готов к работе', '// Техническое задание готово'), caps-with-underscore link labels ('НА_ГЛАВНУЮ'), bracketed hero tagline, `andrey@portfolio:~$` prompts. The privacy policy shifts to careful legalese and speaks in the first person as an individual, not a company ('Андрей Караваев (далее — «я», «специалист», «разработчик»)'), which is quietly reassuring — a real person taking responsibility rather than a fake agency 'we'. Overall the copy is the site's second-strongest asset after the certificates: nothing is overclaimed, and the one thing that would normally be hidden (the age) is simply stated.
standout_features:
Ranked by borrowability for a conventional software-engineer portfolio.

THE HEADLINE IDEA — WORTH STEALING WHOLESALE:
1. **THE SPEC BUILDER (`/tor_builder.html`) AS THE PRIMARY CTA.** Instead of 'Contact me', the site offers 'Составить ТЗ за 10 минут' — a 35-question adaptive wizard that produces a formatted technical specification. Mechanics worth studying: question 1 branches the entire remaining flow by project type (Сайт / Веб-приложение / Telegram-бот / Telegram-бот + Сайт / 'Свой вариант / не знаю' with a free-text escape), and each branch has its own question set (`site_*`, `webapp_*`, `bot_*`, `botsite_*`) plus shared closing questions for deadline, budget and contact preference; every step declares `type` (single/multi/text), `required`, and a `show()` predicate, so conditional questions appear only when relevant (e.g. `site_cabinet_desc` only if a user cabinet was selected, `bot_db_what` only if a database was chosen). Progress is persisted to `localStorage` under `tor_quiz_v5` so an interrupted session resumes; a top bar shows a fill bar, ten tick marks and an '01 / 01' step counter; a custom confirm modal guards the restart. `generateTZ()` then assembles an indented plain-text document with a title, project type, description, a per-branch feature section, and a 'Общие параметры' block covering timeline, budget (formatted `toLocaleString('ru-RU')` + ' руб.'), contact method and free-form notes. WHY IT IS GOOD: it inverts the usual freelance funnel. A normal portfolio asks a stranger to compose an email describing what they want — the highest-friction step in the whole process. This asks multiple-choice questions instead, and the artefact it hands back is useful to the visitor even if they never hire him. It also pre-qualifies (budget floor stated as 1,000 RUB) and pre-structures the lead. Direct analogue for a job-seeking portfolio: a short guided form that produces a role/requirements summary, or simply a structured project-brief generator.
2. **THE CTA DEGRADES CORRECTLY WHEN ITS BACKEND DOES NOT EXIST.** `tor.js` declares `BOT_API_URL = '/send-tor'`, which GitHub Pages cannot serve (verified 404/405) — yet the flow still converts, because the result screen does not depend on it: it renders the generated spec into an **editable `<textarea>`** ('Сформированный текст (можно редактировать)'), offers a 'Скопировать ТЗ' clipboard button, and offers a `https://t.me/andr3ywb?text=<encoded spec>` deep link that opens Telegram with the first 4,000 characters pre-filled. Three lessons in one: keep the primary conversion path serverless so a static host suffices; let the user EDIT the generated output before sending (respects the client and improves the input); and use a messenger deep link with pre-filled text instead of a form POST. The dead endpoint is still a loose end worth removing, but the graceful path means the feature works today.

CHEAP AND WORTH STEALING:
3. **PROVENANCE STATUS BADGES ON EVERY PROJECT CARD** — 'Хакатон · 2 место', 'Хакатон · Участие', 'Коммерческий', 'Пет-проект', 'Соло проект'. Five words per card that tell a reader which work was paid, which was competitive, which was team versus solo. Near-zero cost, large credibility gain, and it solves the 'do I mix pet projects with real work?' problem by labelling rather than hiding.
4. **LINK THE ACTUAL CERTIFICATE, NOT A BADGE.** The terminal's `achievements` output hyperlinks two real award PDFs. Verifiable proof is the single highest-leverage content upgrade available to any early-career portfolio, and it costs one file upload per claim. (Redaction note: his certificate also exposes three teammates' full legal names — see pii_exposure.)
5. **HONEST ROLE ATTRIBUTION** — 'Командный проект, руководил разработкой' on Artifex, matching the four-name certificate. Claiming the role rather than the whole build reads as more credible, not less.
6. **ABSTRACT PER-PROJECT CSS VISUALS INSTEAD OF THUMBNAILS** — an animated node mesh for the P2P messenger, an orbital system for the diary, a 3D-CSS building for the property site, a candlestick chart for the crypto tracker, a sweeping radar for the Rust platform. Each card gets a distinct identity at almost no asset weight, while the real screenshots live one click deeper in the gallery.
7. **A GALLERY MODAL WITH MOBILE IMAGE VARIANTS** — `getImageUrl()` swaps `.png` for `_m.png` below 768px, and the saving is real (1.81 MB → 397 KB). Pinch-zoom, double-tap zoom and drag-pan are implemented properly with passive listeners. For a portfolio whose proof is screenshots, this is the right investment.
8. **A QR-CODE SHARE PAGE (`/qr_code.html`)** — a dedicated page showing a QR for the domain, linked from the footer as 'Поделиться'. Trivial to build, genuinely useful at a hackathon, meetup or client meeting.
9. **A REAL PRIVACY POLICY THAT MATCHES REALITY.** Nine sections with a table of contents, written in the first person as an individual, disclosing exactly what is stored (`localStorage` for spec progress and consent), stating plainly that no analytics or ad tech is used, and voluntarily documenting the client-side device profiling (CPU cores, timing probe, WebGL support) used to tune graphics quality. Disclosing the device fingerprinting nobody would have noticed is a strong trust signal for a site asking strangers for project budgets.
10. **THE TERMINAL AS THE ABOUT SECTION**, auto-run once on 25%-visibility IntersectionObserver, with randomised per-character typing delay, a fake `pip install` sequence for the stack, and a braille spinner for the achievements 'load'. It makes a CV readable as a performance and fits the brand. Caveat below.

TECHNICAL RESTRAINT WORTH NOTING:
11. **AN ADAPTIVE-QUALITY TIER SYSTEM FOR THE WEBGL SECTION** (`cta_shapes.js`): device classification from `hardwareConcurrency` + `deviceMemory` + `getBattery()` (power-save below 20% charge or `saveData`) + a low-end user-agent regex (SM-A1/SM-J, Redmi 0–6, Moto E/G, Realme, Android 4–8) + iOS < 15 + small-viewport detection; then live FPS measurement via `requestAnimationFrame`, frame-time variance analysis to detect thermal throttling, and dynamic render-scale reduction (0.5–1.0). More runtime performance care than most portfolios attempt, and battery-awareness in particular is rare.
12. **A DELIBERATE, COMMENTED `prefers-reduced-motion` BLOCK** in `base.css`, with a note explaining the real-world case it serves.

ANTI-PATTERNS — THE INSTRUCTIVE PART:
13. **`user-scalable=no, maximum-scale=1.0` ON THE HOME PAGE** blocks pinch-zoom (WCAG 1.4.4) — while the gallery modal hand-implements its own pinch-zoom and `/tor_builder.html` correctly allows `maximum-scale=5.0`. A one-line fix.
14. **THE ENTIRE ABOUT SECTION IS JS-GENERATED WITH NO `<noscript>` FALLBACK** — the served HTML contains an empty terminal box, so a no-JS visitor, a crawler that does not execute scripts, and a link-preview bot all see zero biographical content. The information most likely to be searched for is the information least available.
15. **~2.4 MB CRITICAL PATH FOR A STATIC PAGE**, ~95% of it in three avoidable items: a 726 KB unoptimised PNG portrait, 966 KB of variable-TTF fonts that should be subsetted woff2, and a 603 KB **five-year-old Three.js r128** full build loaded render-blocking from cdnjs for one decorative canvas.
16. **BROKEN SHARE METADATA ON A LEAD-GENERATION SITE**: no `og:title`, `og:description`, `og:url` or `og:type`; `og:image` points at an SVG (declared `image/svg+xml` at 1200×630) that most platforms will not render; and the `<title>` is 'Обо мне' ('About me') rather than the name and role. Every shared link therefore previews badly — the cheapest and highest-impact fix on the whole site.
17. **JS MOTION IS UNGATED BY REDUCED-MOTION** — the CSS block is correct but no script checks the preference, so Lenis scroll hijacking, the starfield, the WebGL scene and the character-by-character typing all still run. The terminal in particular should render instantly rather than type when reduce is set.
18. **A DEAD `/send-tor` ENDPOINT** left in the shipped code (404/405 on GitHub Pages), and **typography that changes on the conversion page** (Space Mono + IBM Plex Sans from Google Fonts on `/tor_builder.html` versus self-hosted Unbounded + JetBrains Mono everywhere else) — the page where brand consistency matters most is the one that breaks it.

STRUCTURAL LESSON: this is the inverse of the usual junior-portfolio failure mode. The evidence layer is excellent — linked certificates, four live repos, 34 real screenshots, honest provenance badges — and the conversion mechanism is genuinely inventive. What holds it back is entirely operational hygiene: image and font weight, an obsolete CDN dependency, blocked zoom, missing OG tags, and a bio locked inside an animation. All five are afternoon fixes, which makes this the highest-ROI-remaining site in the set.
originality_vs_template: Fully custom, hand-written, with no template lineage — and the source confirms it rather than merely suggesting it. No generator or framework fingerprints (no Next/Nuxt/Astro/Jekyll/Hugo artefacts, no build output directory, no `node_modules`-derived bundle, no shadcn/Tailwind utility soup, no theme attribution or footer credit), and the file organisation is idiosyncratic in a way templates never are: an `@import`-aggregator `main.css` with a Russian comment explaining its backwards-compatibility purpose, ten hand-scoped single-purpose scripts, bespoke per-project CSS visuals, and a 51 KB hand-authored branching questionnaire in `tor.js`. Only two dependencies are borrowed at all (Lenis for smooth scroll, Three.js r128 for one decorative canvas), both via CDN script tag. The author's own fingerprints are throughout: Russian code comments ('Печатает текст посимвольно в элемент', 'Слайды вставляются автоматичекси' — including its typo), `'use strict'` IIFEs, and a versioned localStorage key (`tor_quiz_v5`) indicating the spec builder has been through five iterations. The overall dark-terminal look is a recognisable genre — GitHub-dark palette, monospace, `//` comment headings — so the aesthetic is conventional even though every line of it is original; the differentiation is carried by the spec builder and the provenance badges, not by the visual style.
source_available: Yes — the site's own source is public at **github.com/Andre-wb/portfolio** (JavaScript, `has_pages: true`, 2 stars, last pushed 2026-06-22, which matches the served document's `last-modified` header exactly). It is the GitHub Pages publishing repo, so the deployed site and the repository are the same artefact — a clean self-dogfooding signal, and it means the spec builder, the adaptive-quality tier system and the gallery implementation are all readable by anyone evaluating him. The repo is not linked or announced from the site itself (the footer and hero link the GitHub *profile*, not the portfolio repo), so the dogfooding is discoverable rather than advertised — a missed one-line opportunity, since 'this site's source' is a strong credential for a client who wants to see code quality. The wider account is genuinely open: 12 public repositories including four of the five showcased projects (`Vortex`, `Artifex`, `Orbityx`, `HotFix`), plus `Stellarix` (Rust, his most-starred at 4), `Dataset-for-StellarixAI`, `near-tools`, `vortex-introduce-page`, `lethalhome` and `TidyTasks`. Licensing was not verified per repository [uncertain — repository licence fields were not individually checked, so it is unclear whether the portfolio source or the project repos carry an explicit open-source licence].
contact_methods: Four channels across four placements, all direct and none gated. The channels: **Telegram** `@andr3ywb` (`t.me/andr3ywb`) — clearly the primary, appearing in the hero social row, the mobile nav, the CTA section as 'Написать напрямую мне', the footer, and as the destination of the spec-builder deep link with the generated specification pre-filled; **GitHub** `github.com/Andre-wb` (hero, mobile nav, footer); **email** `andreykaravaev640@gmail.com` as a live `mailto:` (hero social row, mobile nav, footer Contacts column); and the **spec builder** itself, which functions as the structured contact form (its `contact_type` question asks the client to choose Telegram / Email / Телефон / другой способ and supply the value, which is then embedded in the generated spec). Placement is deliberate and repeated: the hero puts three icon links plus the 'Составить ТЗ за 10 минут →' button above the fold; the fixed header's fourth nav item is 'Нанять'; the CTA section pairs the spec-builder button with a direct-Telegram button; and the footer devotes one of four columns to contacts. No LinkedIn, no VK, no phone number, no scheduling link, no contact form on the home page, and no email-capture or newsletter. The channel mix is well matched to the Russian freelance market (Telegram-first with email as fallback), and offering both a low-friction structured path (the wizard) and a zero-friction direct path (Telegram) side by side is the right pattern for a lead-generation site.
pii_exposure: Moderate on the owner's own data, and — the notable finding — it exposes third parties' full legal names, which no other site in this set does. OWNER, IN CLEARTEXT: a personal Gmail address, `andreykaravaev640@gmail.com`, as a live `mailto:` in three places (hero social row, mobile nav, footer), unobfuscated and trivially scraped; a Telegram handle `@andr3ywb`; the full real name (the personal brand and the domain); a **portrait photograph** (`assets/andrey-photo.png`, 726 KB) prominently in the hero; and — disclosed voluntarily in the terminal — his **age, 16**. The age is the most consequential item: it is not PII leakage in the technical sense but a deliberate self-disclosure that makes him identifiable as a minor on a site that solicits commercial engagements from strangers and shows his face, which carries safeguarding implications well beyond the usual privacy calculus, and may also affect the enforceability of the contracts the spec builder is designed to initiate [uncertain — jurisdictional contract-capacity implications are outside what can be assessed from the site]. THIRD-PARTY PII: the linked `кибер_рывок.pdf` certificate contains the full legal names of three teammates — Мальцев Борис Иванович, Афанасьев Леонид Андреевич, Абдувалиев Дониёрбек — alongside his own full legal name including patronymic (Караваев Андрей Александрович, which also appears in `nuclear_it_hack.pdf`). Publishing a certificate is the right instinct for verifiability, but the version published should have had the co-recipients' names redacted; as shipped, three other people's full legal names are permanently indexable from a stranger's marketing site without any indication they consented. NOT EXPOSED: no phone number, no postal address, no employer, no document or ID numbers, no client name for the commercial project. VISITOR-SIDE PRIVACY IS THE COUNTERWEIGHT AND IS GENUINELY GOOD: zero analytics, zero tracking pixels, zero third-party tracking scripts, no server-side storage of anything (the site is static — spec answers never leave the browser unless the visitor chooses to send them via Telegram or copy them out), a consent banner that accurately describes the only two `localStorage` keys in use, and a privacy policy that voluntarily discloses the client-side device profiling (CPU cores, timing probe, WebGL capability) used for graphics tuning. A visitor filling in a project brief including their budget is not tracked, profiled or emailed — which is a better privacy posture than most commercial lead-gen sites, and stands in deliberate contrast to the owner's openness about his own data.
